opus-5.5.text:
Well, the most fundamental one, I think, is that the code looks right much more often than it is right. These models are extremely good at producing something with the surface statistics of correct code: the right idioms, sensible variable names, a plausible structure. But plausibility and correctness are different things, and the gap shows up exactly where you'd predict, in situations that deviate even slightly from what the model has seen many times before.

If you ask for something that's essentially a common pattern, like a standard data-loading script or a typical web endpoint, you'll usually get something that works, because the model has effectively memorized many variations of it. But if your problem has an unusual twist, a constraint that breaks the usual template, you'll often see the model "snap back" to the familiar version. It solves the problem it expected you to ask rather than the one you actually asked. That's a telltale sign of pattern retrieval rather than reasoning from the specification.

A related failure mode is a lack of consistency across the program. The model can write each function locally fine, but it doesn't maintain a coherent global model of what the program is doing. So you get mismatched assumptions between components: one function assumes the data is sorted and another doesn't guarantee it, or the state is tracked in two different places. A human programmer builds a mental model of the system and derives the code from it. The model is generating token by token from local context, so global invariants tend to drift.

Then there are the hallucinated APIs: functions or arguments that don't exist but would be quite reasonable if they did. That's actually a very revealing error, because it shows the model is interpolating in the space of plausible code rather than grounding itself in what's actually true about the library.

And finally, debugging. When code fails, these systems are often weak at systematically narrowing down why. They'll propose a fix that addresses the symptom, then another, sometimes cycling. Real debugging requires forming a hypothesis, testing it, and updating, which is a kind of on-the-fly adaptation to a novel situation. That's precisely the capability I'd argue these systems are weakest at.

So none of this means they're not useful. They're incredibly useful as a productivity tool, especially for the boilerplate parts of programming. But you have to treat the output as a draft written by something with enormous memory and very little understanding, and you need to be the one who supplies the understanding.

r001.rationale: The response describes inconsistent assumptions between program components, including one function assuming data is sorted. It does not clearly say the model fails to check assumptions against incoming data.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that these models are extraordinarily good at pattern completion. If the code you need looks like code that exists in large quantities on GitHub, you will get something that looks right, often something that is right. And that is precisely where the failure modes come from, because the model is not really reasoning about what the program should do. It is retrieving and recombining templates that are statistically associated with your prompt.

So the first failure mode is what I would call plausible-but-wrong. The code is syntactically perfect, it uses the right libraries, it has the right shape, and it has a subtle bug in the one place where your problem differs from the thousand similar problems in the training data. The model does not know where your problem is unusual. It cannot know, because it has no model of the problem, only a model of the text. And the more fluent the output, the harder those bugs are to spot, because the fluency gives you false confidence.

The second is a kind of brittleness to novelty. If you ask for something that is genuinely new, a data structure or an algorithm that is not a minor variation of something it has seen, the model will typically map it onto the nearest familiar thing and solve that instead. It silently substitutes the problem. This is really the same phenomenon we see in ARC. Performance is high on tasks that are in distribution and collapses as you move away from the memorized patterns, and that collapse is not graceful. You do not get an honest "I don't know how to do this." You get confident, well-formatted nonsense.

The third, and this is more mundane but very common, is hallucinated APIs. Functions that do not exist, parameters that were never there, methods from one library grafted onto another. Again, that is interpolation. The model is averaging over similar APIs and produces something that is a plausible average of them.

And then there is a failure of global coherence. Locally every ten lines are fine, but across a larger piece of code the invariants drift. A variable means one thing at the top and something slightly different lower down. The model has no persistent representation of the program state, so it is reasoning, if you want to call it that, in a sort of sliding window.

What is interesting to me is that these are all the same failure. It is the gap between skill and intelligence. The model has acquired an enormous amount of skill, in the sense of stored solutions, but very little ability to synthesize a new solution on the fly when the stored ones do not quite fit. Intelligence is efficiency in acquiring new skills, in dealing with situations you have not been prepared for. And code is a domain where that gap becomes very visible, because the test of whether the program works is unforgiving. It either runs or it does not.

Now, you can mitigate a lot of this with the right system around the model. If you have test cases, if you have execution feedback, if you do search over candidate programs and verify them, then the model becomes a very useful component. It becomes a prior over the space of programs, which is exactly what you want in a program synthesis system. But that is the key framing. The model is a guess generator, not a reasoner, and the moment you treat its output as reasoned rather than guessed, you get burned.

r001.rationale: The response describes plausible bugs when a problem differs from familiar patterns, but it does not identify unchecked assumptions about incoming data.

astra-6.text:
One failure mode is code that looks plausible locally but doesn’t make sense globally. Each individual function might look reasonable, but the assumptions across functions don’t line up. And sometimes the model solves a slightly different problem from the one you asked it to solve. It recognizes a familiar pattern and produces the standard solution, while missing a constraint that changes the problem.

What makes this tricky is that the output can be very polished. It has comments, sensible variable names, all the surface features of good code. But that doesn’t tell you whether it’s correct. You have to test the actual behavior, particularly the edge cases and the assumptions at the boundaries between components.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions mismatched assumptions across functions and testing edge cases and component boundaries, but does not say generated code relies on assumptions that are unchecked against incoming data.

sol-6.1.text:
One failure mode is that the code looks locally plausible, but it doesn’t quite implement what you asked for. It follows a familiar pattern, uses the right vocabulary, and may even pass the obvious test cases. But there’s an assumption buried in it that doesn’t hold for your problem.

You also see invented APIs, mishandled edge cases, and fixes that address a symptom without addressing the underlying issue. The interesting cases are the subtle ones, because the code can be very readable. Readability gives you a sense of confidence that isn’t necessarily justified.

So I think the key question is: how much work does it take to verify the output? If you can specify the behavior precisely and test it cheaply, these tools can be very useful. If correctness requires understanding a large system and tracking constraints across it, generating a plausible solution is only a small part of the job.

r001.rationale: The response says generated code may contain an assumption that does not hold for the problem, but it does not identify assumptions that go unchecked against incoming data.
